newsitem.title: USA: Iraq's Hamdoon still hopes for deal restart delay.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Hamdoon still hopes for deal restart delay.

text.p: Nizar Hamdoon, Iraq's ambassador to the United Nations, said on Monday that his country still hopes for a delay in the restart date for the second round of the "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations, despite the firm opposition of the U.N. Security Council.
Nevertheless, he said Iraq reserved its position pending approval by the U.N. of its aid distribution plan.
He said the Iraqi mission had delivered on Monday the annexes to the humanitarian aid distribution plan.
The U.N. is expected to complete its review of the plan before the end of the week.

Hamdoon said that his country had been looking for the Secretariat, and the Security Council which has the final say, to interpret resolutions governing the deal in such a way that the latest round would not start until the U.N. Secretary General reported that aid plan was in place.

"Our position is that resolution 1111 (approving the second round in June) endorsed most of the 986 paragraphs (the original deal, approved in May, 1996) including paragraph 13, which is still active," Hamdoon said in a telephone interview with Reuters.
"That says the Secretary General will have to inform the president of the Security Council that all the preparations have been met," Hamdoon said.
However, U.N. officials and diplomats on the Security Council have said for several weeks that that interpretation would not prevail.

Rather, the Security Council decided in discussions last week that it would hold firm in viewing the official start date of the second round as June 8, requiring Baghdad to sell around $1 billion of oil by September 5.
Under the terms of the deal, Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal instalments.

The countries on the U.N.'s Iraq sanctions committee taking most interest, particularly the United States, will allow Iraq to carry over only a small amount of oil sales into the second 90 days, viewing the two-month delay in restarting the second round as due entirely to Iraq.

Hamdoon would not say whether his government would abide by the Security Council position and try to sell its $1 billion allotment by September 5, forego some oil sales from the first round because of the difficulty in selling such a large amount or take some other course of action.
"I cannot comment on that yet. First we will wait for approval of the aid plan and then we will see what is the position of Baghdad," Hamdoon said.
